chunks.title: SPK: read the staining map
chunks.tldr: Pain gone with anaesthetic drop = epithelial problem (but never prescribe anaesthetic). Superior: CL problems, subtarsal FB (linear), floppy lid, SLK, vernal. Interpalpebral: dry eye, neurotrophic, UV. Inferior: blepharitis, exposure, drop toxicity, conjunctivitis, lashes, entropion/ectropion.
points: Other: rubbing, mild chemical, Thygeson (raised, quiet eye).
Remove soft CL before fluorescein.
Non-CL small SPK: PF tears q.i.d. ± gel at night. Large: PF tears q2h + antibiotic ointment, ± cycloplegic.
CL wearer: stop lens; large SPK → fluoroquinolone/tobramycin + ointment at night.
Never patch CL-related SPK.
Ask about snoring/sleep apnoea (floppy lid).

head: Location
Think
rows: CL, FB under lid, floppy lid, SLK, VKC

chunks.hook: Top = lid/lens. Middle = dry/UV. Bottom = blink/blepharitis/bottles of drops.

cards.q: Superior SPK in a snorer with rubbery lids?
cards.a: Floppy eyelid syndrome (associated with obstructive sleep apnoea).

cards.q: Inferior SPK after weeks of frequent preserved drops?
cards.a: Topical drug (preservative) toxicity.

chunks.title: Recurrent corneal erosion
chunks.tldr: Pain on waking, old abrasion or map–dot–fingerprint (EBMD). Acute: cycloplegic + antibiotic ointment ± 5% NaCl, bandage CL if large. Then lubricant/5% NaCl ointment at night for 3–6 months. Refractory: debride, doxycycline 50 mg b.i.d. ± FML, extended bandage CL, stromal puncture (off-axis), diamond burr / PTK (~90%).
points: Causes: EBMD (commonest), Reis–Bücklers, Thiel–Behnke, Meesmann, stromal dystrophies, band, Salzmann, surgery.
Signs may vanish within hours — look for negative staining.
Deep PTK → hyperopic shift.
Follow 1–2 days till healed, then 1–3 monthly.
chunks.hook: Ouch on opening the eyes = erosion. Ointment at bedtime for months.

cards.q: Oral drug used for refractory recurrent erosions?
cards.a: Doxycycline (MMP inhibitor), 50 mg b.i.d.

chunks.title: Dry eye: diagnosis
chunks.tldr: Tear meniscus <0.5 mm, TBUT <10 s, inferior/interpalpebral staining. Schirmer: unanaesthetised normal ≥15 mm/5 min; anaesthetised ≤5 mm abnormal (≤10 borderline). Types: evaporative (MGD, worse mornings) vs aqueous-deficient (worse evenings). Screen Sjögren if dry mouth.
points: Discomfort often out of proportion to signs.

Causes: menopause, connective tissue disease (Sjögren, RA, GPA, SLE), scarring (pemphigoid, SJS, trachoma), drugs (antihistamines, anticholinergics, TCAs, beta-blockers, isotretinoin, SSRIs), lacrimal infiltration, radiation, vit A deficiency (bariatric surgery), after LASIK/PRK/SMILE.
Repeated focal break-up = surface irregularity, not dry eye.
Other tests: tear osmolarity, MMP-9, lactoferrin.
Sjögren → lymphoma risk; multidisciplinary follow-up.
chunks.hook: Schirmer with anaesthetic: 5 or less = dry.

cards.q: Abnormal anaesthetised Schirmer result?
cards.a: ≤5 mm wetting in 5 minutes.

cards.q: Dry eye worse in the morning suggests which type?
cards.a: Evaporative (meibomian gland dysfunction).

chunks.title: Dry eye: treatment ladder & filaments
chunks.tldr: Mild: tears q.i.d. Moderate: PF tears q1–2h + night gel, environment, ciclosporin (1–3 months, start with short mild steroid) or lifitegrast (~2 weeks), punctal plugs (treat blepharitis first). Severe: all of these + moisture goggles, acetylcysteine for mucus, serum tears, scleral lens, lateral tarsorrhaphy. Filamentary keratopathy: pull filaments, treat dryness, acetylcysteine 10%.
points: More than q.i.d. drops → must be preservative-free.
Ciclosporin stings for weeks.
Lifitegrast: stinging, blur, metallic taste.
Plugs: collagen (temporary) → silicone; cautery if they keep falling out.
Oral omega-3/flaxseed optional.
Filaments also from SLK (superior), erosions, patching, ptosis, neurotrophic.
Avoid CL and refractive surgery in significant dry eye (daily disposables may be OK).
chunks.hook: Tears → plugs/ciclosporin → goggles → stitch the corner shut.

cards.q: How long does topical ciclosporin take to work for dry eye?
cards.a: 1–3 months.

cards.q: Treatment of filamentary keratitis?
cards.a: Remove filaments, treat underlying dryness (PF tears, plugs), acetylcysteine 10%; bandage CL if severe.

chunks.title: Exposure keratopathy
chunks.tldr: Poor closure → inferior or band-shaped staining, worse in morning. Causes: VII palsy, sedation/ICU, lid scarring/ectropion, nocturnal lagophthalmos, proptosis (thyroid), after ptosis/bleph surgery, floppy lid, poor blink. Check Bell's phenomenon and corneal sensation. Rx: PF tears, ointment, taping, amniotic membrane → tarsorrhaphy, gold weight, decompression.
points: All sedated/obtunded patients need prophylactic lubrication.
Reduced sensation + exposure = high ulcer risk.
Prokera (ring-mounted amnion) in clinic.
Severe decompensation → conjunctival flap/amniotic graft.
chunks.hook: Can't close + can't feel = cornea in danger.

cards.q: Surgical option for exposure from VII nerve palsy?
cards.a: Upper lid gold/platinum weight or tarsorrhaphy.

chunks.title: Neurotrophic keratopathy
chunks.tldr: Numb cornea → less pain than expected; non-healing inferior oval defect with rolled grey edges → stromal melt, descemetocele, perforation. Causes: HSV/VZV, surgery (LASIK, PK), V nerve lesions (acoustic neuroma), diabetes, PRP, topical NSAIDs/anaesthetic abuse, crack cocaine. Rx: PF tears/plugs → antibiotic ointment/bandage CL → cenegermin (NGF) 6×/day × 8 weeks, amnion, tarsorrhaphy, doxycycline + vit C.
points: Test sensation with cotton wisp before anaesthetic.
Look for zoster scars, VII palsy, absent Bell.
CT/MRI if CNS lesion suspected.
Serum/albumin/cord serum drops; scleral lens (PROSE); corneal neurotisation.
Exposure + neurotrophic rarely heals without tarsorrhaphy.
Severe ulcers: admit (poor compliance, anaesthetic abuse).
chunks.hook: Big defect, little pain = numb cornea.

cards.q: First FDA-approved drug for neurotrophic keratopathy?
cards.a: Cenegermin (recombinant human nerve growth factor) 0.002%, six times daily for 8 weeks.

cards.q: Tumour classically causing neurotrophic + exposure keratopathy?
cards.a: Acoustic neuroma (V and VII involvement).

chunks.title: UV keratopathy & Thygeson
chunks.tldr: UV (welder's flash/sunlamp): bilateral severe pain 6–12 h after exposure, dense interpalpebral SPK. Rx: cycloplegic + antibiotic ointment + analgesia. Thygeson SPK: bilateral recurrent raised stellate grey dots, white quiet eye; mild → tears; moderate → short mild steroid (slow taper), ciclosporin/lifitegrast, bandage CL.
points: UV DDx: toxic keratopathy, thermal burn (curling iron — debride, treat as abrasion), chemical (check pH).
Reliable UV patients can self-check at 24 h.
Thygeson: treatment guided by symptoms; IOP checks on steroids.
chunks.hook: Welded today, screaming tonight. Thygeson = white eye, spotty cornea.

cards.q: When do symptoms of UV keratopathy start?
cards.a: 6–12 hours after exposure.

cards.q: Thygeson SPK lesions look like?
cards.a: Coarse, slightly raised stellate grey-white epithelial opacities in a quiet eye.

chunks.title: Pterygium & pinguecula
chunks.tldr: Pterygium: wing of fibrovascular tissue onto cornea (usually nasal, 3/9 o'clock), Stocker iron line; pinguecula: yellow bump, stays off the cornea. UV/dust. Rx: sunglasses, tears; inflamed → mild steroid/NSAID. Excise if threatens axis, astigmatism, irritation, CL problems, cosmetic, before cataract/refractive surgery — with conjunctival autograft or amnion (MMC for recurrent).
points: Atypical lesion → biopsy (CIN/OSSN, melanoma).
Pseudopterygium: after trauma/ulcer/cicatricial disease; probe passes under; underlying thinning.
DDx: dermoid, peripheral hypertrophic subepithelial degeneration, pannus.
Measure growth every 3–12 months.
chunks.hook: Pterygium flies onto the cornea (wing); pinguecula stays on the shore.

cards.q: Technique that lowers pterygium recurrence?
cards.a: Excision with conjunctival autograft (or amniotic membrane) ± intraoperative mitomycin C.

chunks.title: Band keratopathy
chunks.tldr: Calcium at Bowman's, interpalpebral, clear zone at limbus, Swiss-cheese holes. Common: chronic uveitis (JIA), IK, oedema, phthisis, glaucoma, silicone oil. Less: hypercalcaemia (hyperparathyroid, renal failure, sarcoid, myeloma, vit D), gout. Unexplained → Ca, PO₄, Mg, albumin, U&E, urate. Rx: lubricants or EDTA chelation (debride, rub 3–4% EDTA 10–60 min).
points: Starts at 3 and 9 o'clock near limbus.
After EDTA: antibiotic ointment, cycloplegic, bandage CL.
Residual haze → PTK; can repeat EDTA.
chunks.hook: Band = chalk on Bowman's; EDTA dissolves chalk.

cards.q: Treatment to remove band keratopathy?
cards.a: Epithelial debridement and chelation with disodium EDTA 3–4%.

chunks.title: Bacterial keratitis: recognise & culture
chunks.tldr: White stromal infiltrate + epithelial defect + thinning; can't see iris through it. Assume bacterial until proven otherwise. Common: Staph, Pseudomonas (soft CL, fast, necrotic, hypopyon), Strep (purulent or crystalline in grafts), Moraxella (inferior, deep, debilitated). Culture if >1–2 mm, in visual axis, not responding, or odd story; culture the CL and case too.
points: Hypopyon without perforation is usually sterile.

DDx: fungal (plant trauma, feathery, satellites), Acanthamoeba (pain ≫ signs), HSV, atypical mycobacteria (post-LASIK, indolent; keep LJ plates 8 weeks), sterile marginal (staph), CL sterile infiltrates, rust ring, anaesthetic abuse (ring opacity).
History: sleeping in lenses, water/hot tub, solutions, steroids already given.
Measure infiltrate, defect, hypopyon every visit.
IOP with Tono-Pen.
chunks.hook: Soft lens + fast ulcer + hypopyon = Pseudomonas.

cards.q: When should a corneal infiltrate be cultured?
cards.a: If >1–2 mm, central/visual axis, unresponsive to treatment, or atypical history/appearance.

cards.q: Organism typical of crystalline keratopathy in corneal grafts?
cards.a: Streptococcus viridans.

chunks.title: Bacterial keratitis: treatment by risk
chunks.tldr: Low risk (small peripheral, no stain): FQ or polymyxin/trimethoprim q1–2h awake (CL wearer: FQ). Borderline (1–1.5 mm or with defect): FQ q1h round the clock after loading q5min ×5. Vision-threatening (>1.5–2 mm, central, not improving): fortified tobramycin 15 mg/mL + cefazolin 50 mg/mL (or vanco 25) alternating hourly. Cycloplegic; shield, never patch.
points: Moxi/besifloxacin: better gram +; gati/cipro: better Pseudomonas/Serratia.
Vancomycin: MRSA risk, penicillin/cephalosporin allergy.
Steroids only after organism known and infection controlled (never early with fungus, atypical mycobacteria, Nocardia).
Thinning: doxycycline + vit C.
Oral FQ for scleral extension/perforation risk.
Gonococcus: IV ceftriaxone (cornea) or 1 g IM (conjunctiva only). Haemophilus: oral co-amoxiclav.
Admit: sight-threatening, can't do drops, anaesthetic abuse, IV antibiotics.
Atypical mycobacteria: FQ/amikacin/clarithromycin for weeks + oral clarithromycin.
Response: less pain first; never taper below q.i.d.; reculture if worse; biopsy if negative; glue/graft for perforation.
chunks.hook: Big or central → fortified tobra + cefazolin, hourly, day and night.

cards.q: Fortified antibiotic regimen for a severe bacterial ulcer?
cards.a: Fortified tobramycin (15 mg/mL) alternating with fortified cefazolin (50 mg/mL) or vancomycin (25 mg/mL), each q1h around the clock.

cards.q: Earliest sign that a bacterial ulcer is responding?
cards.a: Reduced pain.

chunks.title: Fungal keratitis
chunks.tldr: Filamentous (Fusarium, Aspergillus): plant trauma or CL, feathery edges, satellites, raised epithelium. Yeast (Candida): sick/steroid-treated eyes, looks bacterial. Stains: Gram, Giemsa, KOH, calcofluor. Rx: natamycin 5% (filamentous), amphotericin 0.15% (Candida), voriconazole 1% q1–2h; stop steroids; ± oral azole; debride; intrastromal injections; therapeutic PK before it reaches limbus.
points: Natamycin is the only commercial topical antifungal; others compounded.
Antifungals penetrate poorly through intact epithelium.
Infiltrate often extends beyond epithelial defect.
Response slow; stability is good news; epithelial healing ≠ cure.
Lamellar keratoplasty contraindicated (recurrence); intracameral antifungal at PK.
chunks.hook: Branch in the eye → fungus with feathers.

cards.q: First-line topical agent for filamentous fungal keratitis?
cards.a: Natamycin 5%.

cards.q: Clinical clues to filamentous fungal keratitis?
cards.a: Vegetable trauma, feathery infiltrate margins, satellite lesions, raised epithelium, slow course.

chunks.title: Acanthamoeba keratitis
chunks.tldr: Soft CL + tap water/swimming/hot tub. Pain far worse than signs. Early: pseudodendrites, epithelial ridges, radial keratoneuritis. Late (3–8 weeks): ring infiltrate. Mimics HSV — any 'HSV' in a CL wearer that won't heal → think Acanthamoeba. Rx: PHMB 0.02% or chlorhexidine 0.02% + propamidine hourly, ± oral azole, miltefosine 50 mg b.i.d./t.i.d. × 4 weeks; months of treatment.
points: Tests: scrapings (Giemsa/PAS cysts, calcofluor), non-nutrient agar with E. coli overlay, biopsy, confocal microscopy.
Miltefosine: check U&E, LFT, pregnancy test; rebound inflammation after stopping.
Stop CL in both eyes; cycloplegic; oral NSAIDs/opioids for pain.
Continue ~3 months after inflammation settles (often 6–12 months total).
PK only after 6–12 months quiet (recurrence).
chunks.hook: Contact lens + tap water + agony + ring = Acanthamoeba.

cards.q: Classic early sign of Acanthamoeba keratitis?
cards.a: Radial keratoneuritis (infiltrates along corneal nerves) with pseudodendrites.

cards.q: Main topical treatments for Acanthamoeba?
cards.a: PHMB 0.02% or chlorhexidine 0.02%, plus propamidine 0.1%.

chunks.title: Crystalline keratopathy
chunks.tldr: Infectious: in grafts/steroid-treated corneas, along sutures — Strep viridans (also CoNS, Corynebacterium, fungi, atypical mycobacteria post-refractive). Schnyder (AD, cholesterol crystals, arcus, check lipids). Bietti (limbal + retinal crystals). Cystinosis (kids, renal failure → cysteamine drops). Paraproteinaemia (myeloma, MGUS → SPEP).
points: Infectious: culture incl. AFB; taper steroid rather than stopping abruptly.
Schnyder: PTK or graft; treat dyslipidaemia; Swede–Finn.
Cystinosis infantile form fatal without renal transplant.
chunks.hook: Crystals in a graft = Strep viridans.

cards.q: Systemic disease with corneal crystals treated with cysteamine drops?
cards.a: Cystinosis.

chunks.title: HSV: the forms
chunks.tldr: Lid vesicles (cross dermatomes, both lids), follicular conjunctivitis, epithelial dendrite (true terminal bulbs, fluorescein-staining) / geographic ulcer = live virus. Stromal (immune): non-necrotising haze or necrotising ulcer. Endothelial (disciform): round oedema + KPs. Also neurotrophic ulcer, uveitis with high IOP + patchy TIDs.
points: Triggers: surgery, fever, stress, menses, URTI, UV, some drops (prostaglandins).
Kids: more severe, bilateral, recurrent.
Dendrite mimics: VZV pseudodendrites (raised, no bulbs), healing abrasion, Acanthamoeba, verticillata, tyrosinaemia.
Check corneal sensation before anaesthetic.
Dilate: rule out retinitis (ARN).
Diagnosis clinical; PCR if unsure; negative HSV-1 antibody helps exclude.
chunks.hook: Dendrite with bulbs = HSV. Raised squiggle without bulbs = zoster.

cards.q: How does a VZV pseudodendrite differ from an HSV dendrite?
cards.a: Raised mucous plaque without central ulceration or terminal bulbs; stains poorly with fluorescein.

cards.q: Herpetic anterior uveitis clue?
cards.a: Raised IOP (trabeculitis) with patchy iris transillumination defects.

chunks.title: HSV: treatment by layer
chunks.tldr: Epithelial: oral acyclovir 400 mg 5×/day (or valacyclovir 500 mg b.i.d./t.i.d.) 7–10 days, or ganciclovir gel 5×/day; no steroids; debridement helps. Stromal, no ulcer: pred acetate 1% 6–8×/day + prophylactic oral antiviral, taper over months. Stromal with ulcer: low steroid + therapeutic oral antiviral. Endothelial: therapeutic steroid + therapeutic antiviral.
points: Geographic: higher oral doses for 14–21 days.
Topical antivirals max 14–21 days (toxicity). Ganciclovir/acyclovir ointment less toxic than trifluridine.
Non-healing after 1–2 weeks: bacterial, Acanthamoeba, toxicity, non-compliance.
Lids/conjunctivitis: self-limited; antivirals shorten.
IOP: aqueous suppressants; avoid prostaglandins.
Recurrent disease: acyclovir 400 mg b.i.d. long term (HEDS).
Adjust for renal function; valacyclovir caution in HIV (TTP/HUS).
Graft for scars after 3–6 months quiet; antiviral ≥1 year after.
chunks.hook: Epithelium = kill the virus. Stroma = calm the immune system (steroid + antiviral cover).

cards.q: Treatment of HSV stromal keratitis without ulceration?
cards.a: Topical steroid (e.g., pred acetate 1%) with slow taper plus prophylactic oral antiviral.

cards.q: Long-term prophylaxis dose after recurrent HSV keratitis?
cards.a: Acyclovir 400 mg twice daily.

chunks.title: Herpes zoster ophthalmicus
chunks.tldr: V1 rash that respects the midline, spares lower lid; Hutchinson sign (nose tip) → eye likely involved. Start oral antiviral within ~4 days of active rash: acyclovir 800 mg 5×/day / valacyclovir 1 g t.i.d. / famciclovir 500 mg t.i.d. × 7–10 days (all eye cases). IV acyclovir if orbit/nerve/retina involved or very sick/immunocompromised.
points: Eye: conjunctivitis, pseudodendrites (mucous plaques), SPK, immune stromal keratitis, neurotrophic, uveitis with sectoral iris atrophy and high IOP, scleritis, retinitis (ARN/PORN), optic neuritis, palsies.
Corneal disease can come weeks–months–years later.
Stromal/uveitis: pred acetate, taper over months–years; avoid prostaglandins.
Retinitis/optic neuritis/palsy: IV acyclovir 10 mg/kg q8h + oral pred; check for CNS vasculitis/stroke.
No systemic steroids if immunocompromised.
Pain: gabapentin/pregabalin, amitriptyline, capsaicin (not near eye).
Contagious to varicella-naïve people (pregnant women!). Shingles vaccine ≥50.
Ask about Ramsay Hunt (VII, hearing). Follow 3–6 monthly long term.
Chickenpox: limbal vesicles; late stromal/neurotrophic keratitis 4–6 weeks later; no aspirin in kids.
chunks.hook: Nose tip spots = eye at risk (Hutchinson).

cards.q: What is Hutchinson's sign?
cards.a: Zoster vesicles on the tip/side of the nose (nasociliary branch) predicting ocular involvement.

cards.q: Oral acyclovir dose for HZO?
cards.a: 800 mg five times daily for 7–10 days.

chunks.title: Interstitial keratitis
chunks.tldr: Non-ulcerating stromal inflammation with deep vessels → later ghost vessels + scars. Causes: HSV (commonest), VZV, congenital syphilis (bilateral, teens), acquired syphilis, TB (unilateral, sectoral), EBV, Lyme, leprosy, Cogan (IK + vertigo + deafness, negative syphilis). Ix: FTA-ABS/TPPA + RPR, IGRA, CXR. Rx: cycloplegic + steroid; treat cause.
points: Congenital syphilis stigmata: saddle nose, Hutchinson teeth, frontal bossing, salt-and-pepper fundus.
Leprosy: beaded corneal nerves, lost eyebrows, iris pearls.
Cogan → ENT + rheumatology (vasculitis/PAN).
Old scars: RGP/scleral lens or graft.
chunks.hook: Ghost vessels = old IK; think syphilis, then HSV.

cards.q: IK with vertigo, tinnitus and hearing loss but negative syphilis tests?
cards.a: Cogan syndrome.

chunks.title: Staph marginal keratitis & phlyctenules
chunks.tldr: Staph hypersensitivity: peripheral infiltrates with a clear zone at the limbus, sectoral redness, little pain/AC reaction, blepharitis/rosacea. Rx: lid hygiene + antibiotic; moderate → steroid with antibiotic cover; recurrent → doxycycline (erythromycin in kids <8). Phlyctenule: white limbal nodule with vessels, can creep onto cornea; kids; staph (rarely TB → IGRA).
points: Infectious infiltrates: round, painful, AC reaction, not multiple/recurrent.
Type IV hypersensitivity to staph antigens.
Doxycycline 100 mg b.i.d. 2 weeks → daily; not in pregnancy/breastfeeding/<8 yrs.
Topical azithromycin/ciclosporin help lid inflammation.
Phlyctenule heals 10–14 days with scar; ciclosporin as steroid sparer.
chunks.hook: Clear gap at the limbus = staph immune reaction, not infection.

cards.q: Key feature distinguishing staph marginal infiltrate from infection?
cards.a: Clear zone between infiltrate and limbus, multiple/recurrent, minimal pain and AC reaction.

chunks.title: Contact lens problems
chunks.tldr: Any CL wearer with pain/red eye: lens out, rule out ulcer; never patch. Others: solution toxicity, deposits, tight lens (no movement, imprint, may get sterile hypopyon), CLARE, PMMA warpage (spectacle blur), neovascularisation, limbal stem cell deficiency (whorl staining at limbus), pseudo-SLK, lost lens in superior fornix.
points: Infiltrate >1 mm, central or odd → culture.
Small infiltrates/SPK: FQ drops + cycloplegic.
Toxicity: stop, PF tears, return in daily disposables or peroxide system.
Tight lens/CLARE: refit flatter, more oxygen-permeable, no extended wear.
Warpage: off lenses 2–6 weeks until refraction stable, then RGP.
LSCD: stop CL, PF lubricants, plugs, short steroid, serum drops, stem cell surgery.
Care: no sleeping in lenses; PF cleaner/saline; hydrogen peroxide disinfection; weekly enzyme if not disposable.
chunks.hook: CL + pain = lens out + look for an ulcer.

cards.q: Signs of tight lens syndrome?
cards.a: No lens movement, 'sucked-on' lens, conjunctival imprint, central corneal oedema, AC reaction ± sterile hypopyon.

cards.q: Early sign of contact lens–related limbal stem cell deficiency?
cards.a: Whorl-like punctate staining near the (superior) limbus.

chunks.title: Giant papillary conjunctivitis
chunks.tldr: Itch, mucus, lens riding high; papillae ≥1 mm on upper tarsus (evert every CL wearer!). Mild: new lenses (daily disposable), less wear, better cleaning. Severe: stop CL 1–4 months, mast cell stabiliser/antihistamine, brief mild steroid (no CL meanwhile). Also from exposed sutures and prostheses.
points: DDx: vernal (young, seasonal, Trantas dots, shield ulcer), atopic (dermatitis, lower lid too).
Ciclosporin/lifitegrast if long-term needed.
Symptoms improve before papillae shrink.
chunks.hook: Flip the lid of every lens wearer.

cards.q: Non-contact-lens causes of GPC?
cards.a: Exposed sutures and ocular prostheses.

chunks.title: Peripheral corneal thinning: the list
chunks.tldr: PUK (painful, with scleritis; RA, GPA, polychondritis, PAN, SLE — may be first sign). Mooren (painful, no scleritis, undermined edge; ?hep C). Terrien (painless, superior, men, lipid line, against-the-rule astigmatism). Pellucid (painless, inferior 4–8 o'clock, bulge above). Furrow (behind arcus, harmless). Plus delle, staph, dry eye melt, exposure/neurotrophic, rosacea.
points: Treat as infectious until cultures negative.
Workup: ESR, FBC, RF, ANA, ANCA, ACE, CXR; scleritis workup; fundus for CWS/posterior scleritis.
Check corneal sensation, Schirmer, lids, papillae.
Inflammatory bowel disease, old HSV/VZV, leukaemia rare causes.
chunks.hook: Painful + scleritis = PUK → find the vasculitis (GPA).

cards.q: Mooren ulcer vs PUK?
cards.a: Mooren: idiopathic, painful, undermined edge, sclera spared. PUK: systemic disease (RA, GPA), sclera often involved.

cards.q: Painless superior peripheral thinning with a lipid line in a man?
cards.a: Terrien marginal degeneration.

chunks.title: PUK treatment
chunks.tldr: Co-manage with rheumatology. Lubricating/antibiotic ointment q2h, cycloplegic, doxycycline + vit C, oral prednisone 60–100 mg (+ gut protection) for progressive thinning, then steroid-sparing immunosuppression (methotrexate, cyclophosphamide/rituximab for GPA). Perforation: glue, patch graft. Avoid topical steroids that thin further.
points: Systemic steroids not used once perforated (glue/graft instead).
PUK signals active, possibly life-threatening vasculitis.
chunks.hook: PUK is a systemic emergency wearing an eye costume.

cards.q: Why is PUK in RA/GPA urgent systemically?
cards.a: It indicates active systemic vasculitis with high mortality if untreated; needs systemic immunosuppression.

chunks.title: Delle
chunks.tldr: Oval limbal thinning next to a bump (chemosis, bleb, pterygium, tumour, after squint surgery) that stops tears spreading → stroma dries. Fluorescein pools; no infiltrate. Rx: ointment q2–4h ± short patch; remove the bump if possible. Thickness normal again in days.
points: Can't remove cause (e.g., bleb): night ointment + viscous tears.
chunks.hook: Bump beside it, dip in the cornea = delle.

cards.q: Mechanism of a corneal delle?
cards.a: Adjacent elevation disrupts tear spread → localised stromal dehydration and thinning.

chunks.title: Keratoconus
chunks.tldr: Teen-onset inferior paracentral thinning + bulge → irregular astigmatism, scissor reflex, egg-shaped mires, Vogt striae, Fleischer ring, Munson sign. Links: eye rubbing, atopy, Down, floppy lid/sleep apnoea, LCA, Marfan. Rx: stop rubbing, glasses → RGP/scleral, cross-linking for progression (≥14 yrs), ring segments, DALK/PK.
points: Topography: inferior steepening; tomography: posterior elevation, thinnest point displaced inferiorly.
DDx: pellucid (inferior band 4–8 o'clock, bulge above, against-the-rule), keratoglobus (whole cornea thin, Ehlers–Danlos, blue sclera), post-LASIK/SMILE ectasia.
CXL (epi-off): riboflavin 30 min + UVA 30 min.
Acute hydrops (Descemet break): pain, oedema; settles ~3 months — cycloplegic, brimonidine, 5% NaCl, steroid; intracameral gas speeds it; not an emergency graft.
chunks.hook: Rubbing makes the cone; cross-linking freezes it.

cards.q: Name three slit-lamp signs of keratoconus.
cards.a: Vogt striae, Fleischer ring, apical thinning/scarring (also Munson sign externally).

cards.q: Treatment to halt progression of keratoconus?
cards.a: Corneal collagen cross-linking (riboflavin + UVA).

chunks.title: Anterior & stromal dystrophies
chunks.tldr: Mostly AD except macular, lattice type 3, CHED (AR). EBMD (map–dot–fingerprint): erosions. Meesmann: tiny epithelial vesicles. Reis–Bücklers/Thiel–Behnke: reticular Bowman opacities, erosions. Lattice: branching lines (type 2 = Meretoja systemic amyloid). Granular: breadcrumbs with clear gaps. Macular: hazy to limbus, cloudy between. Schnyder: crystals + arcus.
points: Lattice, granular, Reis–Bücklers, Avellino = TGFBI family.
Lattice & granular recur in grafts/after PTK within ~5 years.
Macular: thin flat cornea, vision loss more than erosions; recurs late.
Granular II (Avellino) = granular + lattice amyloid.
Treatment: PTK or lamellar/penetrating graft.
chunks.hook: Marilyn Monroe Always Gets Her Lovers in LA: Macular–Mucopolysaccharide–Alcian blue; Granular–Hyaline; Lattice–Amyloid.

cards.q: Which stromal dystrophy is autosomal recessive with opacities reaching the limbus?
cards.a: Macular dystrophy.

cards.q: Lattice dystrophy type 2 is associated with?
cards.a: Meretoja syndrome – systemic amyloidosis with facial and cranial nerve palsies.

chunks.title: Fuchs & other endothelial problems
chunks.tldr: Fuchs: 50s–60s, guttae → stromal then epithelial oedema; blur worse on waking. Rx: 5% NaCl, hair-dryer trick, lower IOP, treat ruptured bullae; DMEK/DSEK when vision falls (DSO in mild). PPCD: vesicles/bands, iris adhesions, glaucoma. CHED: oedema at birth, normal size/IOP, nystagmus. ICE: unilateral, beaten-metal endothelium, PAS, corectopia.
points: Endothelial dystrophy = guttae without oedema (may progress).
Pachymetry, specular microscopy, tomography.
Pseudophakic bullous keratopathy: endothelial damage, vitreous/IOL/tube touch, inflammation; check CME; avoid prostaglandins/adrenergics; EK ± IOL exchange; painful blind eye → PTK, flap, amnion.
chunks.hook: Fuchs: foggy at dawn, clearer by noon.

cards.q: Why is Fuchs blur worse in the morning?
cards.a: Corneal oedema accumulates overnight with lids closed (no evaporation).

cards.q: Preferred surgery for visually significant Fuchs?
cards.a: Endothelial keratoplasty (DMEK or DSEK).

chunks.title: Corneal graft rejection
chunks.tldr: Months–years after PK: red, photophobic, blurry. KPs on donor only, Khodadoust line, oedema, Krachmer spots (subepithelial), epithelial rejection line. Rx endothelial rejection: pred acetate 1% hourly (or difluprednate) ± oral/IV steroid, cycloplegic, IOP control, topical ciclosporin. Epithelial/stromal: double steroids.
points: DDx: suture abscess/infection (remove suture, culture), uveitis (KPs on host too), epithelial downgrowth (doesn't respond to steroid), high IOP oedema, late failure, recurrent HSV/dystrophy.
HSV history → add antiviral.
Treat immediately; taper very slowly, maintain low dose.
chunks.hook: Line of KPs marching across the graft = Khodadoust = rejection.

cards.q: What is a Khodadoust line?
cards.a: Endothelial rejection line of keratic precipitates on a corneal graft.

chunks.title: Refractive surgery types
chunks.tldr: Surface (PRK, LASEK, epi-LASIK): no flap; good for thin corneas/epithelial disease; more pain, slower, haze. LASIK: flap (microkeratome/femtosecond) + excimer; fast, comfortable; flap problems. SMILE: femto lenticule out through small incision; myopia only; no flap; maybe less dry eye.
points: Excimer = argon-fluoride 193 nm UV.
Ranges: PRK −8 to +3; LASIK −10 to +3; SMILE −10 to −1; cylinder ≤3 D.
After refractive surgery IOP reads falsely low (thin cornea).
chunks.hook: PRK peels; LASIK lifts a lid; SMILE pulls a lens out through a keyhole.

cards.q: Main drawback of PRK vs LASIK?
cards.a: More pain, slower recovery and higher risk of subepithelial haze.

chunks.title: Surface ablation & LASIK complications
chunks.tldr: PRK early: bandage CL issues, non-healing defect (HSV?), ulcer, drop allergy; late: haze (↑steroid, PTK + MMC), under/over-correction, steroid IOP rise. LASIK early: dry eye (commonest), flap folds (refloat within 24 h), dislocation (urgent), DLK ('sands of Sahara', day 1–5 → hourly steroid ± lift & wash), infection, CTK. Late: epithelial ingrowth, ectasia (CXL), PISK.
points: PISK: steroid-induced high IOP → interface fluid looks like DLK; central IOP falsely low → measure peripherally; stop steroids, lower IOP.
DLK can appear years later after abrasion/erosion.
CTK: central opacity + flattening; improves over 6–12 months.
Ingrowth: watch if peripheral; debride if dense/threatens flap/vision; YAG for pockets.
Infection: lift flap for cultures; atypical mycobacteria.
Flap sensation reduced 3–12 months.
chunks.hook: DLK gets more steroid; PISK gets less.

cards.q: Diffuse lamellar keratitis treatment?
cards.a: Intensive topical steroids (pred acetate 1% hourly) ± lifting and irrigating the flap if severe.

cards.q: How does PISK differ from DLK in management?
cards.a: PISK is steroid-induced high IOP: lower IOP and taper steroids (opposite of DLK).
